notes.b: A nuclear family is a parent or parents with their dependent children (children who rely on them for support), living together in a self-contained household. It is the standard picture of family in modern Ireland, and each structure has advantages and challenges rather than being better or worse.
points: Two parents, married or cohabiting (living together without being married), and their dependent children form one self-contained household. Marking schemes also accept the wording 'parent or parents and children'.
The unit is small, and the number of children is usually small too, so the household is easy to manage and to keep running on a modest budget.
It is mobile, so members can move for work, which often separates the family from relatives. The family is independent of relatives day to day, but may lack nearby relatives' support.
Tasks, child rearing and decision-making are usually shared between both parents, and often both parents work.
Children depend mainly on the parents' income and on State supports such as Child Benefit.
Advantages: privacy, independence and mobility, because the household answers only to itself.
Drawbacks: less help with childcare and with the care of ill members, and more pressure on the two adults, because there are few other people to share the load.
notes.tip: Give a defining sentence first, then characteristics. Do not write only 'mother, father and children'. Keep nuclear distinct from lone-parent: nuclear has two adults sharing tasks, lone-parent has one.

notes.b: A lone-parent (one-parent) family is one parent living with one or more dependent children. It can arise in several ways, and the parent takes on the work that two adults would normally share.
points: Causes include separation or divorce, the death of a partner (bereavement), desertion, a parent's choice to raise a child alone, and a parent never having lived with a partner.
The lone parent carries the full economic, emotional and practical responsibility, often on one income, which means financial pressure and a heavy workload with little free time.
Most lone parents are women, but fathers can be lone parents too.
Lone parents who work need reliable and affordable childcare, and may depend on relatives, friends or State supports.

The State supports lone parents through social welfare payments and schemes, such as the One-Parent Family Payment (a payment for lone parents) and the Working Family Payment (a payment that tops up low earnings), along with medical cards and childcare supports.
Voluntary organisations also offer lone parents information and support.
Lone parenthood can be temporary, ending when the children grow up or when a new partner joins the household, which creates a blended family.
notes.tip: A lone-parent family is not always a mother with children and not always the result of separation, so list all the causes. Expect to describe pressures: financial, emotional and workload.

notes.b: An extended family is the nuclear family plus wider relatives (relatives beyond the parents and children), often counted in a multi-generation group, and its members stay closely linked and depend on one another. It was the usual form in rural Ireland in the past.
points: Members include grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live in the same household or very close by. Relatives who live far away and are not interdependent do not make an extended family.

A vertical extended family has three or more generations, for example grandparents, parents and grandchildren. A horizontal one has relatives of the same generation, for example brothers with their wives and children.
Members are interdependent, sharing childcare, housework, income and care of older relatives, so costs and tasks are spread widely.
Members may work together as one economic unit, such as a family farm or family business.

There is a strong family tradition, with respect and values passed between generations. Relationships may be more traditional, and historically roles were segregated by gender and age, with men and women carrying out separate tasks.
Households are larger and more crowded, and grandparents often provide much of the childcare.
Advantages: a wide support network and shared costs. Drawbacks: less privacy, and possible conflict between generations and over the authority of older members.
Extended families are the usual form in many cultures, where grandparents often provide much of the childcare.
notes.tip: An extended family is not just any family with relatives. Say that relatives live in the same household or very close by, and are interdependent, sharing childcare, housework and money.

notes.b: A blended (also called reconstituted or step) family forms when a parent with children from an earlier relationship has a new partner, so that two family units join. It begins when the new partner and the children live as one family.
points: Blended families arise through remarriage or cohabitation, and sometimes after the death of a spouse.

Step-parents, step-siblings (no blood link), half-siblings (one shared parent, when the new couple have a child) and extended step-relatives may all be part of the family, creating new relationships. Children may split time between two households.
A joint child of the new partners creates a sibling group that differs in age and background from the earlier children.
The adults must build new relationships and agree rules and discipline, which can be difficult when children have different expectations and routines.
Children may find it hard to accept a step-parent or step-siblings, and rivalry or jealousy can follow. It takes time and patience.
Parents may have financial obligations to children from an earlier relationship as well as to children of the new union, and there are contact arrangements with the non-resident parent.
Advantages: more adults to share income and care, and new relationships and support.
Blended families have become more common in Ireland since divorce became possible and lone-parent families formed new partnerships.
notes.tip: A blended family is not the same as a lone-parent family that gets a new partner. Mention remarriage or cohabitation, step-parents and step-siblings, and the adjustment and rules.

notes.b: Beyond the four main types, examiners accept other contemporary family structures, and naming them can earn extra credit when a question asks for contemporary family structures.
points: Same-sex-parent families have two parents of the same sex and their children, who may come by adoption, fostering, previous relationships or assisted reproduction.
Childless (couple) families are a couple with no children.
Cohabiting-couple families are an unmarried couple, with or without children.
Foster families are children placed in a family's care by the State on a temporary basis.
notes.tip: A question on contemporary family structures wants at least four types, each with a defining feature. Same-sex-parent and childless families give extra credit.

notes.h: Comparing Irish families with European families (settings)
notes.b: Irish families can be compared with families in other European countries in three ways. Differences come from culture, religion, the economy and how far the State supports families.
points: Structure: compare the proportions of nuclear, lone-parent, extended and blended households, using the most recent published statistics from Eurostat and the Central Statistics Office.

Size: compare the number of children and members per family, and how family size has changed since the mid-twentieth century. Ireland has historically had a higher birth rate and larger families than most of Europe, a gap that has narrowed.
Roles: compare who works, who cares for children and who cares for older people.
Roles: Nordic countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Norway provide State-funded parental leave and childcare, which supports shared parenting and mothers' employment.

Roles: in many southern European countries, such as Italy and Spain, the family, including grandparents, often provides much of the childcare and care of older people, and adult children may remain at home longer.
Ireland is a mixture: the nuclear family is the most common household structure, relatives, especially grandparents, are still important for childcare, and care follows a family-based approach.

State support: compare how far each country relies on the State and on the extended family to support parents. In Ireland, State support such as childcare and parental leave has grown but still relies on families and on private spending.
notes.tip: If asked to compare Irish and European families, give one contrast for each of structure, size and roles.

keyTerms.definition: A family of two parents and their dependent children living together in a self-contained household.
A family in which one parent lives with one or more dependent children.
A family that includes parents, children and wider relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins.
A family formed when one or both partners bring children from an earlier relationship into a new union.
A child who relies on parents or guardians for financial support and care.
A partner of a parent who is not the child's biological or adoptive parent.
People who live together under one roof and share living arrangements, which may differ from the family they belong to.
Two unmarried adults living together as a couple.

questions.prompt: Identify and describe two modern family structures.
questions.model: Two structures, each identified and described. Lone-parent family: one parent living with one or more dependent children, arising through separation, bereavement or choice. Blended family: partners with children from earlier relationships, arising through remarriage or cohabitation, with step-relationships and rules to agree. Accept any two of nuclear, extended, lone-parent or blended, with accurate descriptions.

questions.prompt: Compare the characteristics of lone-parent families and extended families, and explain the challenges each type of family may face.
questions.model: Lone-parent family: one parent and dependent children; one income; full economic, emotional and workload responsibility; reliance on childcare and on relatives or State supports such as the One-Parent Family Payment. Challenges include financial pressure, role overload and limited time. Extended family: parents, children and wider relatives living together or nearby; interdependence; shared childcare, housework and money; often one economic unit. Challenges include segregated roles, dependence on the older generation, and conflict over authority and living space. Comparison: the lone-parent family has one adult to share responsibilities, while the extended family has several adults but may have shared expectations to manage.
